core_idea: Material properties determined by structure at all scales (atomic, microstructural, macroscopic); processing controls structure; structure determines properties; performance governed by properties; quantum mechanics provides unified theoretical framework for all material classes.
pioneers: Morris Cohen, Cyril Stanley Smith, Nevill Mott, William Hume-Rothery, A. H. Cottrell, Ernest Orowan
representative_works: ARPA IDL program documents (1960-1962); Journal of Materials Science (1966); Smith A History of Metallography (1960)
institutional_markers: ARPA IDLs at 12 universities (1960-1962) FOUNDING EVENT; Journal of Materials Science (1966); Materials Research Society (MRS, 1973); Acta Metallurgica → Acta Materialia (1996); metallurgy → materials science department renaming 1960s-1990s
controversies: Credit for founding materials science contested among universities; boundary with condensed matter physics and engineering unclear; materials tetrahedron criticized as too simplistic; cross-trunk parentage (also Trunk 8: Engineering)
critical_works: Journal of Materials Science vol. 1 (1966); Cottrell Dislocations and Plastic Flow in Crystals (1953); Smith History of Metallography (1960)
critical_instruments: Electron microscope; X-ray diffractometer; hardness tester; differential scanning calorimeter; synchrotron X-ray sources

label: Quantum Chemistry and Computational Chemistry
description: Application of quantum mechanics to chemical systems; DFT as dominant method. Two overlapping areas: quantum chemistry (Hartree-Fock, post-HF) and computational chemistry (DFT, molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo). MERGE: quantum physics + chemistry + computing. Nobel Chemistry 1998 (Kohn + Pople) marks maturation.
core_idea: Chemical bonding and reactivity determined by quantum mechanical electronic structure; Density Functional Theory reduces many-electron problem to 3D electron density; computation enables calculation of properties impossible analytically; B3LYP functional works for organic chemistry.
pioneers: Walter Kohn, John Pople, Robert S. Mulliken, Axel Becke, Gerhard Ertl, Martin Karplus
representative_works: Hohenberg-Kohn DFT (1964); Kohn-Sham (1965); Gaussian software (1970s); Becke B3LYP (1993)
institutional_markers: Nobel Chemistry 1966 (Mulliken), 1998 (Kohn + Pople); Journal of Computational Chemistry (1980); GAUSSIAN software; Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation (2005)
controversies: DFT Nobel Chemistry not Physics (Kohn was physicist); GAUSSIAN software commercial restrictions criticized; B3LYP overuse (most cited paper ever but applied outside validity range); machine learning replacing DFT for some applications
critical_works: Kohn Nobel lecture (1999); Cramer Essentials of Computational Chemistry (2004); Szabo and Ostlund Modern Quantum Chemistry (1989)
critical_instruments: High-performance computers; NMR spectrometers (validation); X-ray crystallography (structure validation)

label: Surface Science and Interface Chemistry
description: Physical and chemical phenomena at surfaces and interfaces at atomic/molecular level. Ultra-high vacuum techniques and surface-sensitive probes (LEED, XPS, Auger, STM). Bridge between heterogeneous catalysis and condensed matter physics. Ertl resolved Haber-Bosch mechanism at atomic level (Nobel 2007).
core_idea: Surface atoms have different coordination and electronic structure from bulk; surface-to-volume ratio dominates at small scales; reaction mechanisms on surfaces differ from solution; clean surface experiments under UHV reveal elementary reaction steps.
pioneers: Gerhard Ertl, Gabor Somorjai, Gerd Binnig, Heinrich Rohrer, Kai Siegbahn
representative_works: Ertl N2 on Fe Haber-Bosch mechanism papers (1970s-1980s); Binnig-Rohrer STM (1982); Siegbahn ESCA (1967)
institutional_markers: Surface Science journal (Elsevier, 1964) FOUNDING MARKER; American Vacuum Society; Nobel Chemistry 2007 (Ertl); Nobel Physics 1981 (Siegbahn XPS), 1986 (Binnig-Rohrer STM)
controversies: Applicability of single-crystal model surface results to industrial supported catalysts (Somorjai pressure gap, materials gap); STM initially doubted; surface vs bulk distinction blurred at nanoscale
critical_works: Ertl reactions at surfaces papers (Science, Angewandte Chemie); Somorjai Chemistry in Two Dimensions (1981)
critical_instruments: Ultra-high vacuum chamber; LEED (Low Energy Electron Diffraction); STM; AFM; XPS (ESCA); Auger electron spectrometer

label: Nanotechnology
description: Science, engineering, and technology at 1-100 nm scale — where quantum effects, surface chemistry, and classical mechanics all simultaneously matter. Not a single discipline but a scale. STM (1981) enabled; fullerenes (1985), CNTs (1991), graphene (2004) as landmark materials. National Nanotechnology Initiative (NNI, 2000) institutionalized. ACTIVE field — still rapidly developing.
core_idea: At nanoscale (1-100 nm), materials exhibit size-dependent properties differing from bulk; surface-to-volume ratio determines behavior; quantum confinement effects become significant; nanoscale structures are both building blocks and functional devices.
pioneers: Gerd Binnig, Heinrich Rohrer, Richard Smalley, Robert Curl, Harold Kroto, Sumio Iijima, Don Eigler, Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov
representative_works: Feynman There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom (1959 lecture); Binnig-Rohrer STM (1982); Kroto et al. C60 (1985); Iijima CNTs (1991); Geim-Novoselov graphene (2004)
institutional_markers: Nanotechnology journal (IOP, 1990); NNI USA (2000) $500M/year; Nano Letters (ACS, 2001); NSECs (NSF, 2001); Nobel: C60 1996, STM 1986, graphene 2010; EU Graphene Flagship (2013, €1B)
controversies: Drexler molecular assembler concept vs Smalley objections; NNI hype cycle; health risks of engineered nanoparticles; definition of "nanotechnology" contested; military applications
pioneer_ids: PION_228, PION_229, PION_230, PION_231, PION_232, PION_233, PION_234
critical_works: Feynman lecture (1959); Drexler Engines of Creation (1986); Ratner Nanotechnology: A Gentle Introduction (2003)
critical_instruments: STM; AFM; electron microscope (HRTEM); atomic layer deposition; electron beam lithography

label: Semiconductor Physics and Microelectronics
description: Application of solid state physics to semiconductor devices. Transistor (1947) → integrated circuit (1958-1959) → Moore's Law scaling → modern computing. Core physics: band theory, p-n junctions, carrier dynamics, quantum tunneling at sub-5nm nodes. Bridges physics, materials science, electrical engineering.
core_idea: Semiconductor band structure determines electronic properties; p-n junctions enable charge carrier control; transistor switches/amplifies via majority carrier modulation; miniaturization follows Moore's Law with quantum effects dominating below ~5nm.
pioneers: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, William Shockley, Jack Kilby, Robert Noyce, Gordon Moore, Herbert Kroemer, Zhores Alferov
representative_works: Bardeen-Brattain transistor (1947); Shockley Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors (1950); Kilby IC (1958); Kroemer heterostructure laser (1963)
institutional_markers: Transistor 1947 (Bell Labs) FOUNDING EVENT; Nobel Physics 1956 (Bardeen-Brattain-Shockley), 2000 (Kilby, Kroemer, Alferov); IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (1952); Semiconductor Industry Association (1977); ITRS/IRDS roadmaps
controversies: Shockley credit-taking from Bardeen-Brattain; Silicon Valley spawned by Shockley's behavior (traitorous eight); Moore's Law as self-fulfilling prophecy vs physical law; EUV lithography feasibility debates 2000s-2010s
critical_works: Shockley Electrons and Holes in Semiconductors (1950); Sze Physics of Semiconductor Devices (1969); Mead and Conway VLSI Systems (1980)
critical_instruments: Photolithography; molecular beam epitaxy (MBE); ion implantation; atomic layer deposition; EUV scanner

label: Polymer Science and Soft Matter Physics
description: Study of macromolecules (polymers, colloids, liquid crystals, gels, biological soft matter) and their physical properties. Straddles organic chemistry, physical chemistry, and condensed matter physics. Nobel: Staudinger 1953 (macromolecules), Ziegler-Natta 1963 (polymerization), Flory 1974 (polymer theory), de Gennes 1991 (soft matter).
core_idea: Long chain molecules have unique statistical mechanical properties (random coil, reptation); polymer physical properties determined by chain statistics; soft matter systems share slow dynamics, sensitivity to entropy, and mesoscale structure.
pioneers: Hermann Staudinger, Paul Flory, Pierre-Gilles de Gennes, Karl Ziegler, Giulio Natta, Wallace Carothers
representative_works: Staudinger macromolecule concept (1920s); Flory Statistical Mechanics of Chain Molecules (1969); de Gennes Scaling Concepts in Polymer Physics (1979)
institutional_markers: Journal of Polymer Science (1946); ACS Polymer Division (1950s); Nobel: Staudinger 1953, Ziegler-Natta 1963, Flory 1974, de Gennes 1991
controversies: Staudinger macromolecule concept initially rejected by Wieland and other chemists (1920s-1930s); reptation model (de Gennes 1979) vs constraint release models; polymer melts chain statistics debate (Flory vs de Gennes)
critical_works: Flory Principles of Polymer Chemistry (1953); de Gennes Scaling Concepts in Polymer Physics (1979); Edwards The Theory of Polymer Dynamics (1986)
critical_instruments: GPC (gel permeation chromatography); NMR (polymer structure); light scattering; rheometer; DSC (differential scanning calorimeter)

label: Biochemistry and Structural Biology (Physical Methods)
description: Chemistry and physics of living systems — primarily in Trunk 5 (Biology), but deeply connected to Trunk 3 via physical methods: X-ray crystallography (DNA 1953, proteins 1957-1960), NMR spectroscopy, cryo-electron microscopy, and computational molecular dynamics. Trunk 3 claims the physical/chemical methods contribution.
core_idea: Structure of biological macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids) determines function; physical methods (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM) reveal structure at atomic level; computational MD simulates dynamics; Trunk 3 physical chemistry tools revolutionized biology.
pioneers: Max Perutz, John Kendrew, Martin Karplus, Michael Levitt, Kurt Wüthrich, Joachim Frank
representative_works: Watson-Crick DNA structure (1953, Franklin X-ray data); Kendrew myoglobin (1958); Perutz hemoglobin (1960); Karplus MD simulation (1977)
institutional_markers: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (Cambridge, 1962); Nobel: Perutz-Kendrew 1962, Sanger 1958+1980, Wüthrich 2002, Frank 2017; PDB (Protein Data Bank, 1971)
controversies: Rosalind Franklin credit for DNA X-ray data (Photo 51) not acknowledged in Nobel (Watson-Crick-Wilkins 1962); Trunk 3 vs Trunk 5 node ownership; cryo-EM resolution revolution obsoleting crystallography in some areas
critical_works: Perutz and Kendrew protein structure papers (1958-1960); Karplus MD paper (1977); Frank cryo-EM Nobel lecture (2017)
critical_instruments: X-ray crystallography (synchrotron); NMR spectrometer (high-field); cryo-electron microscope; high-performance computers for MD

label: 2D Materials and Topological Quantum Materials
description: Two-dimensional materials (graphene, TMDs, van der Waals heterostructures) and topological quantum materials (topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, topological superconductors). Active/emerging frontier — Nobel Physics 2010 (graphene), 2016 (topological phases). Dedicated journal 2D Materials (IOP, 2014).
core_idea: 2D materials have properties qualitatively different from bulk (Dirac fermions in graphene, valley polarization in TMDs); topological invariants classify quantum phases of matter; topology protects surface states against disorder; moiré superlattices engineer new quantum phases.
pioneers: Andre Geim, Konstantin Novoselov, David Thouless, Duncan Haldane, J. Michael Kosterlitz, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero
representative_works: Geim-Novoselov graphene (2004); TKNN invariant paper (1982); Haldane model (1988); magic-angle graphene (2018)
institutional_markers: Nobel Physics 2010 (Geim-Novoselov graphene), 2016 (Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz topological); 2D Materials journal (IOP, 2014); EU Graphene Flagship (2013, €1B)
controversies: Magic-angle graphene superconductivity mechanism (Mott insulator vs BCS-like); topological insulator material synthesis challenges; 2D semiconductor vs Si CMOS competition
critical_works: Novoselov et al. Science (2004); TKNN Physical Review Letters (1982); Kane-Mele topological insulator (2005)
critical_instruments: STM; ARPES (Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy); van der Waals heterostructure assembly; millikelvin dilution refrigerator

label: Quantum Computing and Quantum Information
description: Use of quantum superposition, entanglement, and interference for computation and communication. Feynman concept (1982); Shor algorithm (1994) established importance for cryptography; Google/IBM superconducting qubit hardware race; Preskill NISQ era (2018). EMERGING — no stable technology platform. Google Willow error correction milestone (2024).
core_idea: Quantum bits (qubits) exploit superposition and entanglement to enable exponential parallelism for certain problems; Shor algorithm threatens RSA; error correction below threshold enables scalable fault-tolerant computation; different physical platforms (superconducting, trapped ion, photonic) all viable.
pioneers: Peter Shor, David Wineland, John Preskill, Alain Aspect, John Clauser, Anton Zeilinger
representative_works: Shor algorithm (1994); Nielsen-Chuang textbook (2000); Preskill NISQ paper (2018); Google Willow (2024)
institutional_markers: Nielsen-Chuang textbook (2000); IBM Quantum Experience (2016, public cloud access); National Quantum Initiative Act (USA, 2018); Nobel Physics 2022 (Aspect-Clauser-Zeilinger entanglement); npj Quantum Information (2015); Quantum journal (2017)
controversies: Google "quantum supremacy" (2019) disputed by IBM; practical usefulness of NISQ era qubits uncertain; timelines for cryptographically relevant quantum computer highly uncertain (5-50 years); which hardware platform will win
pioneer_ids: PION_240, PION_241, PION_242, PION_243, PION_244, PION_245
critical_works: Shor algorithm (1994); Nielsen-Chuang (2000); Preskill NISQ (2018)

label: Astrochemistry and Extreme-Conditions Chemistry
description: Chemistry under extreme conditions — interstellar space (ultra-low density, radiation, cryogenic temperatures) and high pressure (diamond anvil cell, megabar range). Two subfields: astrochemistry (molecular abundance in ISM, planetary atmospheres) and high-pressure chemistry (new phases, metallic hydrogen, room-temperature superconductors under pressure).
core_idea: Chemical species stable under extreme conditions differ fundamentally from those at ambient conditions; quantum chemistry predicts exotic species unobservable in normal laboratory; high pressure creates new phases with novel properties; interstellar medium chemistry is dominated by ion-molecule reactions and dust surface processes.
pioneers: William Klemperer, Ewine van Dishoeck, Neil Bartlett, Mohamed Eremets, Arthur Moulton
representative_works: Bartlett noble gas chemistry (1962); diamond anvil cell papers (1959+); van Dishoeck interstellar chemistry reviews
institutional_markers: Icarus journal (astrochemistry, 1962); IAU astrochemistry working groups; diamond anvil cell technology (1960s); Nobel: Bartlett-related discovery (no direct Nobel but noble gas compounds landmark)
controversies: Room-temperature superconductivity under pressure claims (many disputed); high-pressure hydrogen metallization timeline; interstellar molecular abundances calculation accuracy; astrochemistry vs cosmochemistry boundary
critical_works: van Dishoeck Interstellar Chemistry Special Issue (2006); Mao-Bell diamond anvil cell review; Journal of Chemical Physics extreme conditions papers
critical_instruments: Diamond anvil cell; radio telescope (molecular line emission); Hubble/JWST spectrograph; high-pressure apparatus
